  ### Git Worktrees Explained

  A Git worktree allows you to link multiple working directories to a single repository. Traditionally, working on multiple branches requires cloning the repository again or constantly stashing
  uncommitted changes and switching branches. Git worktrees eliminate this friction by enabling you to check out different branches simultaneously into separate, dedicated folders on your local
  filesystem.

  Under the hood, all linked worktrees share the same central Git directory and object database. This architecture saves significant disk space, avoids redundant network operations, and ensures
  that commits or branches created in one worktree are immediately accessible across all others. Each worktree maintains its own index, HEAD pointer, and working files, allowing you to edit, stage,
  and test code independently.

  Worktrees shine in daily workflows such as handling urgent production hotfixes while mid-feature, reviewing peer pull requests, or running long build processes in parallel without interrupting
  ongoing development. You manage them effortlessly using commands like git worktree add <path> <branch>, inspect active instances with git worktree list, and clean them up safely using git
  worktree remove <path>.

  By completely removing context-switching overhead and preventing clutter from duplicate clones, Git worktrees provide an elegant, remarkably efficient solution for multitasking across branches in
  modern software development workflows.
